questions.question: When `c()` receives values of several basic types, which type does the resulting atomic vector get?
options: The type of the first value, which then fixes the type of the whole vector.
The type that occurs most often among the values passed to `c()`.
The type furthest along logical, integer, double, character among the inputs.
None: R stops with an error until all values have the same type.

questions.question: Which of these explicit conversions never turns a value that is not missing into `NA`?
options: `as.numeric()`, since every value can be written as a number
`as.integer()`, since it drops decimals instead of failing
`as.logical()`, since every value counts as `TRUE` or `FALSE`
`as.character()`, since every value can be written as text

questions.question: Which of these calls returns a vector of type double?
options: `c(1L, 2L, TRUE)`
`as.integer(c(2.5, 3))`

questions.question: What does R print for `c(2.50, "x", FALSE)`?
What does `TRUE + TRUE + FALSE` return?
options: `[1] TRUE`
an error, because logical values cannot be added

questions.question: What happens when R runs `as.numeric(c("4", "4.5", "n/a"))`?
options: It returns `[1] 4.0 4.5  NA` silently, with no warning and no error.
It returns `[1] 4.0 4.5 0.0` and prints `NAs introduced by coercion`.
It stops with an error, because `"n/a"` cannot be turned into a number.
It returns `[1] 4.0 4.5  NA` and prints the warning `NAs introduced by coercion`.

questions.question: What does `m <- cbind(c(1, 2), c("a", "b")); m[1, 1] + 1` give?
options: `[1] 2`, because R turns `"1"` back into a number
the error `non-numeric argument to binary operator`
`[1] "2"`, because the result stays character
`[1] "11"`, because `+` joins the two as text

questions.question: What does `x` print after `x <- c(2.5, 4, 7); x[2] <- TRUE`?
options: `[1] TRUE TRUE TRUE`

questions.question: What does `x` print after `x <- c(5, 10); x[2] <- "ten"`?
options: an error, because `x` is a numeric vector

questions.question: Why does `c(1L, 0.5)` become a double vector rather than an integer vector?
options: Doubles always win because R stores all numbers as doubles internally.
The last value in `c()` decides the type, and here it is the double 0.5.
An integer vector would overflow, so R switches to double for safety.
Every integer can be written as a double, but 0.5 cannot be an integer without loss.

questions.question: A column of prices typed into R as `c(3.5, 4, "missing", 2)` contains one text entry. Which consequence does this have?
options: Only that entry becomes `NA`, and R prints a warning about it.
The whole vector becomes character, silently, so arithmetic on it fails later.
R drops the text entry and keeps the three prices as numbers.
R stops immediately with an error, because prices must be numeric.

questions.question: Which statement correctly contrasts implicit coercion (as in `c()`) with explicit coercion (with `as.*()` functions)?
options: Implicit coercion only moves up the ladder and is silent; explicit coercion can move down and may give `NA`.
Implicit coercion may give `NA` with a warning; explicit coercion always succeeds without a message.
Both only move up the ladder, so neither can ever produce an `NA`.
Explicit coercion only moves up the ladder; moving down requires implicit coercion.

questions.question: What does `c(typeof(TRUE + TRUE), typeof(TRUE + 1))` return?
options: `[1] "logical" "double"`
`[1] "double" "double"`
`[1] "integer" "double"`
`[1] "integer" "integer"`

questions.question: What does `m <- rbind(c(1, 2), c(TRUE, FALSE)); m[2, ]` return?
options: `[1]  TRUE FALSE`
`[1] "TRUE"  "FALSE"`

questions.question: What does `x * 2` return after `x <- c(2, 8); y <- c(x, "z")`?
options: an error, because `x` became character as well

questions.question: For each invoice $i$, the logical vector `late` records whether it was paid late, and the numeric vector `amount` holds its amount $a_i$, in the same order. What does `sum(late * amount) / sum(late)` compute?
options: The share of all invoices that were paid late.
The average amount of the invoices paid on time.
The average amount of the invoices paid late.
The average amount of all invoices, late or not.

questions.question: `as.numeric(TRUE)` returns `1`, but `as.numeric("TRUE")` returns `NA` with the warning `NAs introduced by coercion`. Why?
options: `"TRUE"` is text that is not a number; `TRUE` = 1 holds only for logical values.
`as.numeric()` reads only digits, so it rejects any value written in capital letters.
A string must first be converted with `as.integer()` before `as.numeric()` can read it.
`as.numeric()` cannot convert logical values either; the `1` is a printing artefact.

questions.question: What does `as.character(c(TRUE, 3L, 2.5))` return?
What does `m <- cbind(c(2, 4), c("a", "b")); as.numeric(m[, 1]) + 1` return?
options: `[1] NA NA`, with the warning `NAs introduced by coercion`
the error `non-numeric argument to binary operator`

questions.question: What does R return for `as.integer(c(2.9, -2.9))`?
options: `[1] NA NA`, with the warning `NAs introduced by coercion`
